articleSummary: Japanese encephalitis (JE) outbreaks in Vietnam, with Hanoi reporting the first 2026 case: a 13-year-old resident of Hung Dao Commune, Quoc Oai District, who had completed three primary vaccine doses but missed the booster per schedule. A separate fatal JE case in Thanh Hoa Province involves 14-year-old N.T.T.L. from Dong Son Ward, Thanh Hoa City; initial fever, headache, vomiting, and fatigue progressed to speech difficulty and altered consciousness; lab-confirmed JE; died despite intensive care and vasoactive support. Vaccination schedule: primary three-dose series (1st at age 1; 2nd 1–2 weeks later; 3rd one year after 2nd) with boosters every 3–4 years until age 15, plus mosquito-control measures and prompt care if symptoms arise after travel to risk areas.

articleSummary: A 32-year-old man from Vinh Long Province developed severe chickenpox with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and hemoconcentration on day 4 of illness. Varicella zoster virus causes chickenpox, transmitted via respiratory droplets or direct contact with vesicles, with up to 90% attack rate in non-immune individuals. articleSummary: As of mid-May 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has recorded 202 Ebola deaths and 875 laboratory-confirmed cases, a case-fatality rate of about 23%. Uganda has 19 cases and 2 deaths amid spread of the rare Bundibugyo Ebola virus lineage into neighboring regions. The World Health Organization and Africa CDC have declared both international and continental public health emergencies of international concern, reflecting the outbreak's severity and cross-border risk. Transmission is via direct contact and exposure to bodily fluids, with containment proving extremely challenging because there is no widely available vaccine or specific therapy for Bundibugyo. Africa CDC, an African Union public-health agency established in 2016 and launched in 2017, coordinates regional response and strengthens member states' outbreak capabilities.

articleHeadline: Covid Making Comeback In Mumbai? Why H1N1, RSV And Viral Infections Are Rising Before Monsoon
articleSummary: Viral respiratory infections are rising in Mumbai ahead of the monsoon, with Covid-19, H1N1, other influenza A viruses, and RSV circulating simultaneously. Breach Candy Hospital’s lab reports more than seven positive cases daily of either Covid-19 or H1N1. Hospital admissions include one Covid patient each at Breach Candy and Bhatia Hospital on Saturday; OPD records show several new Covid cases daily. The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation acknowledges the uptick, attributing it to weather changes—delayed monsoon, unusually high humidity, and stagnant air that may keep viruses suspended longer. Case numbers are expected to decline with sustained rainfall clearing the atmosphere. The current Covid infections are largely mild, but vulnerable groups—elderly, pregnant women, and those with diabetes or chronic lung disease—remain at higher risk, and overlapping infections may worsen outcomes by weakening lung interstitial tissues.
notes: ムンバイにおけるCOVID-19、H1N1、RSV、インフルエンザAの同時流行が報告されている。Breach Candy Hospitalでは毎日7件以上の陽性症例が報告されており、流行しやすさが高い。ただし、現在の感染は主に軽症であり、重症度の基準には該当していない。モンスーン開始により症例数は減少が予想されている。脆弱性が高い集団（高齢者、妊婦、糖尿病患者、慢性肺疾患患者）へのリスクは継続。続報を注視する必要がある。

articleHeadline: At Least 30 Die in Congo Displacement Camp as Ebola Fears Grow
articleSummary: At least 30 people have died since early May in the Kigunze displacement camp near Bunia, Ituri province, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, fueling fears of an Ebola outbreak. Some victims are believed to have Ebola, but authorities cannot confirm the cause for all deaths because many patients and families refused medical testing. Ten people were buried in the past week, indicating an unusually high toll. The DRC has faced multiple Ebola outbreaks in its eastern provinces, where conflict, weak healthcare, and mass displacement hinder containment. In Kigunze, overcrowding, poor sanitation, and limited access to clean water heighten transmission risk. Ongoing funding shortages for water, sanitation, and healthcare programs amplify vulnerability. Relief agencies urge urgent support to bolster health services, sanitation facilities, and disease surveillance to prevent further loss of life.

articleSummary: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 247 deaths among 956 confirmed cases (case fatality rate 25.8%). Hospital isolation includes 316 patients, with 92 recoveries. Declared May 15 in Ituri, a border province with Uganda and South Sudan, the outbreak has spread to North and South Kivu. Uganda reports 19 confirmed cases, 14 imported from the DRC, including two deaths. The Bundibugyo strain is involved, with a typical fatality of 30–50% and no approved vaccine or specific treatment. WHO warns of substantial regional risk; the outbreak was designated a public health emergency of international concern in May. This is the third-worst Ebola outbreak on record, after 2014–2016 West Africa and 2018–2020 eastern DRC outbreaks. Transmission occurs via direct contact with bodily fluids, causing fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and internal hemorrhages.

articleSummary: As of June 21, 2026, Israel is managing a patient suspected of Ebola virus disease who arrived from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Mongwalo village, May 25, 2026). Israeli hospitals follow explicit EVD procedures: all general hospitals will triage in emergency departments for rapid isolation of a suspected case, with full PPE for staff and minimal patient contact. If life-saving actions are required, they are performed with maximum protection. Upon fever or exposure in Africa, the patient wears a surgical mask, companions are limited, and the patient is isolated in a dedicated room pending evaluation. Five hospitals with high readiness—Sheba, Tel HaShomer; Ichilov; Hadassah Ein Kerem; Soroka; Rambam—can activate a special emergency room, conduct exam and laboratory testing, and send Ebola diagnostics to the Biological Institute per protocol. Evacuation is by MDA. Other hospitals notify the National Hospitalization Center to arrange transfer.

articleSummary: Indonesia's IDAI warns that children are the most vulnerable to death from dengue fever (DENV). In dengue cases, the 15–44 age group accounts for about 42% of cases, but mortality is highest among 5–14-year-olds at about 40%, compared with 30% for 15–44-year-olds. Dengue is caused by four serotypes; a child may be infected by other serotypes after an initial infection, with potentially more severe illness on subsequent infections. Important warning signs in children include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, lethargy, rising hematocrit, and falling platelet counts, with hematocrit rise highlighted as particularly dangerous. Hartono Gunardi, head of IDAI’s Immunization Task Force, cites a fatal case resulting from delayed hospital care during the critical third day of fever, underscoring the urgency of early recognition and care.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Do adults contract hand, foot, and mouth disease?
articleHeadline: Người lớn có mắc tay chân miệng không?
articleSummary: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) can affect adults in Vietnam, not just children. Transmission is mainly fecal–oral and via contact with secretions, saliva, mouth ulcers, vesicles, or contaminated objects such as toys and door handles; caregivers and healthcare workers have higher risk without proper hand hygiene. In Vietnam, HFMD is caused by non-polio Enteroviruses, most commonly CV-A16, CV-A6, and EV71. Adults may present with fever, sore throat, fatigue, and vesicles on the hands, feet, knees, elbows, or in the mouth; EV71 can cause severe complications including meningitis, encephalitis, brainstem dysfunction, seizures, altered consciousness, and rarely myocarditis or respiratory failure. Over half of adult EV71 infections can be asymptomatic yet transmissible, with household transmission about 52%—highest among siblings. Prevention stresses regular handwashing and surface cleaning. Vietnam offers HFMD vaccination for children 2 months to <6 years with ~97% protection; VNVC plans rollout soon.

articleSummary: Trichinellosis in Argentina prompts reinforced winter controls. articleSummary: Bangladesh faces a worsening dengue outbreak as of 21 June 2026, with 9 dengue-related deaths and 4,900 total cases this year, including 220 new hospitalisations in the last 24 hours. In 2025, the country reported 102,861 dengue cases and 413 deaths. Health authorities note no dengue vaccination programme is currently planned. The health minister said the vaccine is used only in a limited number of countries (Brazil, Malaysia, Australia, Thailand) and lacks global approval; WHO and UNICEF consultations will guide any future decision. Dengue is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; symptoms include high fever, headaches, body pains, nausea, and rashes; most recover in 1–2 weeks, but severe cases require hospital care.

articleHeadline: Τροπικές νόσοι "αποικούν" την Ευρώπη μέσω των κουνουπιών - Πώς θα προφυλαχθούμε
articleSummary: Rising humidity, shifting rainfall and higher temperatures extend mosquito-borne transmission seasons, enabling tropical pathogens to colonize Europe. Dengue fever, West Nile virus, and Chikungunya are highlighted as key mosquito-transmitted threats, with Aedes aegypti identified as the primary vector. From early 2025 through mid-August, three EU/EEA countries reported dengue cases: France, Italy, and Portugal; Greece has only imported cases with no local transmission. A UK study in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface shows Chikungunya could be transmitted at as low as 14°C, underscoring emerging risk where Aedes albopictus—the tiger mosquito—is not yet fully established; risk rises if it becomes established across more areas. articleHeadline: Distrust, misinformation have fuelled disease outbreaks around the world this year
articleSummary: Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, hantavirus on a cruise-ship outbreak in the United States, and diphtheria in Australia illustrate how distrust and misinformation hinder outbreak response. In DRC, rumours and low trust in health services impeded case identification and timely care; unrest near Ebola treatment centers followed a May ban on large funeral wakes, complicating control efforts. For hantavirus, delayed and less visible public messaging by the CDC allowed influencers and social media to spread misinformation about pandemic potential and unproven treatments. In Australia, the diphtheria surge exposed information gaps in remote, overcrowded communities where vaccination uptake and access to care are uneven. The piece calls for transparent, consistent communication—acknowledging what is known and unknown—frequent updates, and locally trusted messengers. Strategies include press conferences, diverse media, and upskilling community organizations and leaders to build trust and improve outbreak response.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola: Why Some Survivors Haven't Finished with the Disease?
articleHeadline: Ebola : pourquoi certains survivants n'en ont pas fini avec la maladie ?
articleSummary: In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ebola outbreaks have continued since May, with 808 cases and 192 deaths (case fatality rate 24%), transmitted through direct contact with bodily fluids or contaminated objects. There is no approved specific therapy; supportive rehydration and symptom treatment improve survival, while several blood-derived or immune-modulating approaches are under study. A JAMA Neurology study in Liberia (2015–2023) followed 229 people—148 survivors and 81 uninfected contacts—evaluating neurological function every six months. During acute illness, survivors reported headaches, altered consciousness, and stroke-like or meningitis-encephalitis symptoms; years later, memory loss, irritability, and concentration difficulties remained more common. Interestingly, those with more severe initial disease tended to have fewer long-term neurological sequelae, while higher anti-Ebola antibody levels linked to more symptoms, suggesting immune-driven damage rather than persistent virus. The findings underscore Ebola as neurotropic and call for routine neurological screening in survivor care.

articleSummary: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and COVID-19 are contrasted amid renewed Ebola concerns. Ebola spreads mainly through direct contact with infected body fluids or contaminated surfaces, with outbreaks historically in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda. COVID-19 spreads primarily through airborne droplets and aerosols, enabling spread. Symptoms differ: Ebola causes high fever, severe weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, and possible internal or external bleeding; COVID-19 causes fever, cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, fatigue, and loss of smell or taste. Fatality rates for Ebola have ranged roughly 25%–90% depending on strain and care; COVID-19 fatalities are lower but higher in total cases. Treatments: early use of Ebola regimens like Inmazeb and Ebanga with supportive care; COVID-19 relies on antivirals, oxygen, steroids, and vaccines. Vaccines exist for both; prevention includes PPE, isolation, and Ebola vaccination during outbreaks, and vaccination plus masks for COVID-19. India and others are boosting surveillance and airport screening.

articleHeadline: Estudo encontra fungo Sporothrix em animais atropelados no PR | CNN Brasil
articleSummary: Paraná, Brazil — Researchers identified Sporothrix fungi, agents of sporotrichosis, in wild vertebrates killed by vehicles on highways BR-376 and PR-445 in the Mata Atlântica. Analyzing 81 road-killed animals (2017–2023), they detected DNA from three pathogenic Sporothrix species: S. brasiliensis (main zoonotic Brazilian outbreak agent), S. schenckii, and S. globosa. Eleven animals tested positive, with fungal DNA in internal organs (heart, liver, lungs, spleen), indicating systemic infection. The study includes the endangered southern wild cat (gato-do-mato-do-sul); fungi were also found in birds, challenging the belief that high body temperature prevents fungal infections. Led by the Universidade Estadual de Londrina (Department of Preventive Veterinary Medicine) since 2016, with PUC-PR and Utrecht; funded by FAPESP; published in Mycopathologia. Highlights One Health, wildlife sentinels for zoonoses. Brazil’s roadkill rate (~15 animals/sec; ~1.3 million daily) underscores biodiversity loss.
notes: 記事はパラナ州の野生動物からスポロトリックス菌が検出された研究成果に関するもの。S. brasiliensisはブラジルの既知の人獣共通感染症であり、野生動物が保菌源となることは確認されたが、現在の人への流行や新規集団発生は記述されていない。動物と人の両方が影響カテゴリに含まれており、長期曝露リスク（高い動物死傷率）と流行のしやすさ（人獣共通感染）で基準を満たすが、緊急度は低い。続報で人への感染増加報告があれば再評価が必要。

articleSummary: Trans-boundary animal diseases (TADs) threaten India’s livestock-led economy, with 13 of 17 recognized TADs already present and annual losses of 1–1.5 lakh crores, including FMD (Rs 20,000 crores), LSD (Rs 20,254 crores in 2022-23), and African swine fever (Rs 2,800–14,000 crores). articleHeadline: Can Ebola Spread Through Air? Separating Facts from Myths
articleSummary: Ebola, caused by orthoebolaviruses (formerly ebolavirus), can cause severe illness and death; first identified in 1976 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and is found primarily in sub-Saharan Africa. As outbreaks rise in parts of Africa, myths about airborne spread persist. Ebola is not classified as airborne: transmission mainly occurs through direct contact with an infected person, animal, or deceased person, via blood or other bodily fluids (saliva, vomit, urine, feces, sweat, breast milk, semen) or contaminated surfaces or medical equipment. Airborne transmission is not supported in real-world settings; virus-containing droplets exist only under highly controlled lab conditions. Mosquitoes do not spread Ebola. Early outbreaks often involve exposure to infected wildlife, particularly fruit bats. Healthcare workers protect themselves with PPE (gown, gloves, mask, face shield) to prevent exposure to fluids and potential droplets. Public education helps combat misinformation and guide prevention.

articleHeadline: 10 Key Facts on Hantavirus and Ebola Virus
articleSummary: Canada notes: Hantavirus is nationally notifiable with about 4–5 confirmed cases annually, usually from rodents in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia; Andes strain can spread person-to-person. Americas strains cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome; European/Asian strains cause hemorrhagic fever and kidney dysfunction. Incubation 2–4 weeks; symptoms include fever, headache, myalgia, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis relies on serology and PCR, performed at the National Microbiology Laboratory in Winnipeg; there is no antiviral or vaccine, so treatment is supportive. IPAC is essential; suspected Andes cases require airborne, droplet, and contact precautions with infectious diseases input and public health notification. Ebola virus disease has caused sporadic Central and West African outbreaks since 1976, with fruit bats as reservoirs and transmission via bodily fluids or contaminated surfaces. The current DRC outbreak is Bundibugyo ebolavirus, with a fatality rate of 30–50%. Incubation 2–21 days; symptoms include fever, fatigue, myalgia, GI distress; diagnosis by PCR. Testing advised for travelers or exposures. IPAC must be stringent; vaccines exist for Zaire ebolavirus and antivirals can reduce mortality, but none for Bundibugyo; care remains supportive.
